AI-assisted peer review: efficiency for reviewers, burden for authors—a narrative review
A
M
Asaad Ma Babker
† *
Department of Medical Laboratory Sciences, College of Health Sciences, Gulf Medical University, Ajman, United Arab Emirates
Article metrics
View details
Abstract
Artificial intelligence (AI) in scholarly peer review has the potential to simplify the work of editors and reviewers through faster triage, automated reporting completeness checks, and scalable synthesis of reviewer comments. However, it also presents practical, ethical, and technical limitations that may place implementation burdens on authors. I examine bias arising from training data and model architecture, confidentiality risks from commercial AI deployment, accountability gaps when human judgment is displaced, and the growing threat of hallucinated citations to scientific integrity. I further analyze how poorly governed AI integration shifts remediation and formatting burdens onto authors—particularly those from under-resourced or non-Western institutions. I propose hybrid human–AI workflows, mandatory disclosure standards, and equity-conscious implementation frameworks to address these harms. Responsible AI integration in peer review requires transparency, human accountability, and deliberate protection of the diversity of voices represented in scientific literature. These considerations also extend beyond individual actors to recursive feedback loops in which AI-assisted manuscripts are evaluated by AI-assisted review systems, reinforcing the need for human contextual stewardship.

1 Introduction
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed various aspects of scientific research, including academic publishing and peer review. Large language models and other AI tools have proven in recent years to be capable of automating many tasks that have historically been performed by human editors and reviewers. Automated language and grammar checks, plagiarism detection, format compliance, and even preliminary evaluation of research significance are some of these applications (
Doskaliuk et al., 2025
).

7.6 Limitations and caveats
Nevertheless, these efficiency gains must be carefully balanced against substantive risks. Cognitive offloading—the tendency to delegate analytical effort to AI systems—can erode the depth and independence of human judgment over time, with reviewers placing excessive trust in algorithmically generated assessments even when errors are present (
Gerlich, 2025
). Additionally, the systemic biases inherent to AI models trained predominantly on English-language and Western-institution data risk propagating methodological and geographic prejudices into reviewer feedback (
Hosseini and Horbach, 2023
). These considerations collectively underscore the irreplaceable role of human judgment and ethical accountability as foundational imperatives within any AI-augmented peer review paradigm (
Walshe et al., 2025
).
8 How AI in peer review complicates implementation for authors
While AI-assisted peer review promises efficiency gains for editors and reviewers, it can simultaneously create significant implementation burdens for authors—particularly those from under-resourced or non-Western institutions. Beyond administrative and formatting demands, authors face a deeper and more consequential set of complications rooted in confidentiality risks, algorithmic bias, intellectual property vulnerability, and systemic epistemic inequity, each of which is examined below.

9 Conclusion
AI in peer review offers real efficiency gains for editors and reviewers, but these benefits can impose downstream costs on authors through false positives, algorithmic bias, opaque feedback, and undisclosed AI use. Published evidence of fabricated citations, prompt-sensitive bias, and variable agreement with human reviewers demonstrates that efficiency without accountability can threaten scientific integrity (
Walters and Wilder, 2023
;
Suleiman et al., 2024
;
Liang et al., 2024a
;
Teixeira, 2025
).
Responsible integration demands transparency about AI use, human accountability for all editorial decisions, and equity-conscious design that prevents burden transferring onto authors least equipped to absorb it. Journals should mandate AI disclosure, conduct regular bias audits, and establish author feedback mechanisms to monitor false-positive burdens.
Without these safeguards, AI-assisted peer review risks narrowing the diversity of voices, methods, and knowledge systems that science depends upon. AI can strengthen peer review—but only when governed with the same rigor science demands of the research it evaluates. Governance must also address the recursive author–AI–reviewer feedback loop at the system level, preserving human contextual stewardship as a deliberate safeguard against self-reinforcing errors and epistemic narrowing (
Biele and Kowalski, 2026
).
